title: Consistency model

definition.text: A consistency model is a contract between the programmer and a system: if the programmer follows the rules for operations, reads, writes and updates behave predictably.

facts.text: Consistency models are used in distributed data stores such as filesystems, databases, optimistic replication systems and web caching.

In a store where row X is replicated on nodes M and N, the model decides whether client B, reading from N after client A wrote to M, will definitely, definitely not, or cannot count on seeing the write.
Models define rules for the apparent order and visibility of updates, and they sit on a continuum with trade-offs.
One model is stronger than another if it requires all the other's conditions and more; a model with fewer constraints is weaker.
Strict consistency is the strongest model: every write must be seen instantaneously by all processors, which makes it only a thought experiment because instantaneous message exchange is impossible.
Replicas keep a system reliable and fast, but copies can drift; synchronous replication gives tight consistency, yet applying global synchronization to keep all copies consistent is costly.
Weakening the consistency restrictions decreases the cost of global synchronization and improves performance.

notes: Hardware memory-model sections (weak ordering, release, entry, relaxed write-to-read, transactional memory) are CPU-level and not drafted.

title: Sequential consistency
article: Consistency model#Strong consistency models > Sequential consistency

definition.text: Sequential consistency requires that the result of any execution is as if all operations ran in one sequential order, with each process's operations in its program order.

facts.text: A write need not be seen instantly, but writes by different processors must be seen in the same order by all processors.
Sequential consistency has no notion of time or of the most recent write, and it is weaker than strict consistency.
Lamport proposed it in 1979.
It can produce non-deterministic results, because the interleaving of operations between processors can differ from run to run.

title: Linearizability
article: Consistency model#Strong consistency models > Sequential consistency

definition.text: Linearizability, also called atomic consistency, is sequential consistency with a real-time constraint.

facts.text: Each operation has a begin time and an end time, and linearizability adds this real-time constraint to sequential consistency.
An execution is linearizable if every operation can be placed at a single point between its begin and end time while the order still guarantees sequential consistency.
In an atomically consistent store, the sum of the read delay and the write delay is at least the message delay.
Most stronger models, linearizability among them, are trivially eventually consistent, which shows that eventual consistency is a weak guarantee.

notes: No separate Linearizability page was crawled; the entry rests on two sentences in the Sequential consistency section plus the PACELC and Eventual consistency pages. Listed in gaps.

title: Causal consistency
article: Consistency model#Strong consistency models > Causal consistency

definition.text: Causal consistency weakens sequential consistency by splitting events into causally related ones and unrelated ones, and only the related writes must be seen in the same order.

facts.text: Hutto and Ahamad defined it in 1990 as a weakening of sequential consistency.
If event b takes effect from an earlier event a, every process sees b after a.
Writes that are potentially causally related must be seen by all processes in the same order, while concurrent writes may be seen in a different order on different machines.
Two writes are causally related when the processor doing the second write has just read the first, whether the writes came from the same processor or from different ones.

definition.text: Session guarantees are four consistency models proposed in a 1994 paper for the case where a single user or application makes the data modifications.

facts.text: Client-centric models like these can deal with inconsistencies at lower cost in data stores that have no simultaneous updates.
Monotonic reads: once a process reads a value of item x, every later read of x by that process returns the same or a more recent value.
Monotonic writes: a process's write to x completes before its next write to x.
Read-your-writes: a value a process wrote to x is always available to that process's next read of x.
Writes-follow-reads: a write to x that follows a read of x by the same process takes place on the same or a more recent value than the one read.

definition.text: Eventual consistency is a model used in distributed computing to achieve high availability: if no new updates are made to an item, all reads eventually return its last updated value.

facts.text: If no new updates are made to a data item, eventually all read accesses to that item return the last updated value.
Eventual consistency is also called optimistic replication, and a system that has reached it is said to have converged, or achieved replica convergence.
It is a weak guarantee, and until an update converges different queries for a record may see different values.
Eventual consistency gives only a liveness guarantee, that reads eventually return the same value, with no safety guarantee, so any intermediate value is allowed before convergence.
Eventually consistent services are often described as BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency), in contrast to traditional ACID.
Asynchronous replication helps achieve eventual consistency, but it can also leave data inconsistent.
Many NoSQL databases use eventual consistency to offer availability and partition tolerance at the price of reduced data consistency.
Critics say it adds complexity: wrong assumptions about consistency levels cause subtle bugs that only appear during network failures or high concurrency.

definition.text: To converge, an eventually consistent system exchanges updates between servers and reconciles concurrent updates by choosing a final state.

facts.text: Replicas converge through anti-entropy, which exchanges versions or updates of data between servers, and through reconciliation, which chooses a final state when concurrent updates have occurred.
The most appropriate way to reconcile depends on the application.
A widespread approach is last writer wins, and some use first writer wins where last writer wins is unacceptable.
Another approach is to invoke a user-specified conflict handler.
Timestamps and vector clocks are often used to detect concurrency between updates.

Reconciliation must happen before the next read: read repair fixes an inconsistency when a read finds it, write repair fixes it during a write and slows that write, and asynchronous repair runs outside reads and writes.
In an AP database, the nodes are typically re-synced to repair all inconsistencies once a partition is resolved.

definition.text: Strong eventual consistency adds a safety guarantee to eventual consistency: any two nodes that have received the same set of updates, in any order, are in the same state.

facts.text: Plain eventual consistency is only a liveness guarantee: updates will be observed eventually, but nothing is promised about the values seen before convergence.
Strong eventual consistency adds the safety guarantee that any two nodes holding the same unordered set of updates are in the same state.
A common way to ensure it is conflict-free replicated data types.

definition.text: Eventual consistency ensures that updates to a distributed database are eventually reflected across all nodes, and four patterns help applications achieve it.

facts.text: In the event-based pattern, services emit events and other services listen to them to update their own databases, which keeps services loosely coupled but delays consistency.
In the background-sync pattern, a background job makes data across databases consistent, so consistency arrives more slowly because the job runs on a schedule.
In the saga pattern, a sequence of local transactions each updates data in a single service, which manages long-lived transactions that are eventually consistent.
In the CQRS pattern, reads and writes go to separate, eventually consistent databases whose read and write models can each be tuned.

title: PACELC

definition.text: PACELC extends the CAP theorem: during a network partition choose between availability and consistency, and otherwise choose between latency and consistency.

facts.text: If there is a partition (P), the trade-off is between availability (A) and consistency (C); else (E), even in normal operation, it is between latency (L) and consistency (C).
The reason for the latency trade-off is that consistent operations need a full network round trip on reads and writes, while low-latency systems relax consistency to reduce delay.
PACELC addresses a limit of CAP: ignoring the consistency-latency trade-off is a major oversight, because it is present at all times while CAP matters only during a partition.
By CAP's own wording a database counts as available if a query returns after 30 days, a latency no real application accepts.
The four configurations are PA/EL, PA/EC, PC/EL and PC/EC; PC/EC gives firm ACID-style consistency and PA/EL gives high availability and low latency with a more complex consistency model.
PA/EC and PC/EL systems give only conditional guarantees of consistency, so the developer must still write code for the cases where the guarantee is not upheld.
PC does not mean fully consistent; it means the system does not lower consistency below its baseline during a partition and reduces availability instead.

Marc Brooker argues CAP is most relevant where devices connect intermittently, such as IoT and mobile apps, while for cloud applications PACELC is more appropriate because it also covers latency versus consistency without partitions.

notes: Daniel Abadi first described it in a 2010 blog post (e225d0ea19c1); Singh's PACELC chapter (chunk 02) is cited here rather than drafted again.

title: PACELC database classifications

definition.text: PACELC rates databases by whether they favour availability or consistency during a partition and latency or consistency otherwise.

facts.text: The default versions of early Amazon Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak are PA/EL: they give up consistency for availability during a partition and for lower latency in normal operation.
Fully ACID systems such as VoltDB/H-Store, Megastore, MySQL Cluster and PostgreSQL are PC/EC, and Bigtable and HBase are PC/EC too.
MongoDB can be classified as PA/EC: in the baseline case the system guarantees reads and writes to be consistent.
Amazon DynamoDB follows a strong leader model with read-after-write consistency, and its SDKs read eventually consistently by default, while a consistent read returns a current view or an error.

conflicts.text: MongoDB and Redis resolve network partitions by maintaining consistency while compromising on availability.
conflicts.note: The CAP theorem article treats MongoDB as choosing consistency in a partition (PC), the opposite of PA.

notes: The same page lists Cosmos DB both among PA/EL defaults (40e1f893eecb) and as formally CP with five tunable levels (5a6213a1fe03); Cosmos DB is left out. MongoDB: PACELC article says PA/EC, CAP article and Singh say it keeps consistency in a partition; see conflicts and the CP, AP and CA entry.

definition.text: The CAP theorem is often misunderstood: the simple '2 of 3' wording can mislead, and the theorem covers only a narrow case.

facts.text: The '2 of 3' formulation is useful, but as a simplification it can mislead.
Brewer's 2012 clarification says designers need to sacrifice consistency or availability only in the presence of partitions, and that partition management and recovery techniques exist.
CAP prohibits only a tiny part of the design space: perfect availability and consistency in the presence of partitions, which are rare.
The theorem is about 100% availability and consistency; a more realistic discussion weighs latency against consistency when there is no partition, as PACELC does.
Consistency in CAP differs from consistency in ACID transactions, and availability in CAP differs from high availability in software architecture.
Choosing a database purely on CAP is not enough: companies do not pick Cassandra for chat just because it is an AP system, but for a list of other characteristics.
The ByteByteGo guide still finds CAP useful because it opens a set of trade-off discussions, but says it is only part of the story.

title: Primary-backup replication
article: Consistency model#Consistency and replication > Consistency protocols > Primary-based protocols > Remote-write protocols

definition.text: In primary-backup replication, each data item has one primary that coordinates its writes, and backups copy the updates.

facts.text: In the simplest primary-based protocol, write operations are forwarded to a single server while reads can be performed locally.
A write is forwarded to the primary, which sends the update to the backups, waits for acknowledgements from all of them, and then acknowledges completion to the client.

The trade-off is that the client may wait long for the acknowledgement; a non-blocking variant updates locally first and asks backups later, which is faster but does not guarantee the backups are consistent.
The protocol orders all incoming writes, so all processes see writes in the same order, and blocking protocols guarantee that processes see the result of the last write.

notes: Source calls this a remote-write protocol; the local-write variant (primary copy moves to the writing process) is not drafted.

title: Quorum-based replication
article: Consistency model#Consistency and replication > Consistency protocols > Replicated-write protocols > Quorum-based protocols

definition.text: In quorum-based replication a client must get permission from several servers before it reads or writes replicated data.

facts.text: Unlike primary-based protocols, replicated-write protocols carry out all updates on all replicas, and voting is one way to do this.
For a file replicated on N servers, an update needs agreement from at least N/2 + 1 servers, after which the change is applied and a new version number is assigned.
To read, a client asks N/2 + 1 servers for the file's version number, and the read completes if all received version numbers are the most recent version.

title: Active replication
article: Consistency model#Consistency and replication > Consistency protocols > Replicated-write protocols > Active replication

definition.text: In active replication, every replica has a process that applies each update as an operation, and all replicas must apply updates in the same order.

facts.text: A process is associated with each replica to perform the write, and updates reach each replica as an operation to execute.
All updates must be performed in the same order on all replicas, so a totally-ordered multicast mechanism is required.
Implementing such multicast in large distributed systems raises a scalability issue.

An alternative sends each operation to a central coordinator, the sequencer, which assigns a sequence number and forwards the operation to all replicas, but this does not solve the scalability problem either.

title: CAP theorem

definition.text: The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, says a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance.

facts.text: A distributed data store can provide at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance, the three properties commonly desired when designing distributed web services.
Consistency means every read receives the most recent write or an error, so all clients see the same data at the same time whichever node they connect to.
Availability means every request received by a non-failing node must get a response, without any guarantee that the response holds the most recent version of the data.
Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes.
No distributed system is safe from network failures, so partitions generally have to be tolerated, and during a partition one must choose between consistency and availability.

Choosing consistency, the system returns an error or times out when it cannot guarantee fresh data; choosing availability, it always answers with the most recent version it has, even if that may be stale.
In the absence of a network partition, both availability and consistency can be satisfied, and during normal operation a data store covers all three.
Gilbert and Lynch proved Brewer's conjecture in 2002 for the asynchronous network model, then discussed solutions to the dilemma in the partially synchronous model.

title: CP, AP and CA systems

definition.text: Because a distributed database must tolerate partitions, it is classed as CP if it keeps consistency, AP if it keeps availability, or CA if it assumes no partitions.

facts.text: The physical network cannot be guaranteed stable, so a distributed database must choose partition tolerance, which leaves a trade-off between consistency and availability.

A CA database gives consistency and availability across all nodes but cannot do so if any two nodes are partitioned, so it offers no fault tolerance; PostgreSQL and MariaDB are examples, and no NoSQL database is classed as CA.
A CP database gives consistency and partition tolerance at the expense of availability: when a partition occurs, it shuts down the non-consistent node until the partition is resolved.
MongoDB and Apache HBase are CP examples, and etcd also favors consistency over availability during a network partition.

An AP database gives availability and partition tolerance at the expense of consistency: all nodes stay available during a partition, but those on the wrong side may return an older version of the data.
Once the partition is resolved, an AP database typically re-syncs the nodes to repair inconsistencies; Cassandra, CouchDB and ScyllaDB are AP examples.
Databases built on ACID guarantees, such as relational ones, choose consistency over availability, while systems built on BASE, common in NoSQL, choose availability over consistency.
Most modern distributed databases offer configuration options for both consistency and availability.

conflicts.text: MongoDB can be classified as a PA/EC system.
conflicts.note: The PACELC article puts MongoDB on the availability side during a partition, while the CAP article and Singh put it on the consistency side.

notes: MongoDB is CP here (CAP article and Singh agree); the PACELC article's PA/EC rating is recorded in conflicts. Singh lists PostgreSQL and MariaDB as CA while the PACELC article rates PostgreSQL PC/EC; the two frameworks define the terms differently, so this is not recorded as a conflict.
